propositions.text: I dismiss this appeal.
propositions.quote: I dismiss this appeal.

propositions.text: The appellants are Indian citizens fearing persecution from Tamil Nadu police accusing the PA of terrorist links.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant/PA), XXXX XXXX, and XXXX XXXX XXXX (Associate Appellants) are citizens of India. The Appellants fear persecution from the police in Tamil Nadu who accused the PA of receiving funding from foreign terrorist groups and being affiliated with the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE).

propositions.text: The PA alleges he will be apprehended upon return to India for violating conditional release.
propositions.quote: The PA further alleges that he will be apprehended upon a return to India for violating his conditional release.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal and states the appellants are Indian citizens fearing persecution from Tamil Nadu police accusing the PA of terrorist links and apprehension risk.

propositions.text: The PA alleges he was detained for four days in 2007 by Tamil Nadu police Q Branch.
propositions.quote: The PA alleges that he was detained for four days in 2007 by the Q Branch of the Tamil Nadu police.

propositions.text: The PA alleges he was asked to identify two LTTE suspects but did not go after cousin's warning about uncle's disappearance.
propositions.quote: The PA alleges that he was then asked to come to the prison to identify two LTTE suspects but didn't go after his cousin advised him that his uncle had received the same request and did not return.

propositions.text: The PA travelled to England and stayed there until 2013.
propositions.quote: The PA then travelled in England and stayed there until 2013.

paragraphs.summary: The PA alleges detention in 2007, refusal to identify LTTE suspects after a warning, and residence in England until 2013.

propositions.text: The PA returned to India in 2013 and reopened his business, later partnering with a Sri Lankan businessman.
propositions.quote: The PA returned to India and reopened his XXXX business in 2013. After facing financial difficulties, he partnered with a Sri Lankan businessman who he had met in England.

propositions.text: Politically connected individuals opened a competing business called XXXX XXXX.
propositions.quote: The PA alleges that politically connected individuals also opened a XXXX business called XXXX XXXX.

propositions.text: In 2018, a complaint was made against XXXX XXXX, the PA was blamed, assaulted, and threatened.
propositions.quote: In 2018, someone claiming to be from the Appellant's company made a complaint about XXXX XXXX to the police. The PA was blamed for this complaint and was assaulted and threatened as a result.

paragraphs.summary: The PA returned to India, reopened business, faced competition, and was blamed, assaulted, and threatened after a complaint in 2018.

propositions.text: The PA was arrested in 2018, accused of foreign terrorist funding, and questioned about his English business partner.
propositions.quote: The PA was arrested by the Tamil Nadu police on XXXX XXXX, 2018. He was told that his business was supported by foreign terrorist funds. The police also asked about his friend and business partner in England, whom they alleged is a supporter of the LTTE.

propositions.text: The PA alleges detention for three days, threats, release after bribe, and weekly police reporting.
propositions.quote: The PA alleges that he was detained for three days and threatened that the case would be handed over to the Q branch. The PA was released after paying a bribe, although he was required to return to the police station weekly.

propositions.text: The PA and family moved to Bangalore, went into hiding, police sought him at home, then left India for Canada.
propositions.quote: He and his family moved to Bangalore and went into hiding. He alleges the police came to find him at his home when he was in hiding. The Appellants then left India and travelled to Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The PA was arrested, detained, threatened, released after bribe, went into hiding, and then left India for Canada.

propositions.text: The RPD found credibility and internal flight alternative (IFA) in Mumbai were determinative issues.
propositions.quote: The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) found that the determinative issues were credibility and an internal flight alternative (IFA) in Mumbai.

propositions.text: The Appellants argue the RPD erred on credibility and that no IFA exists in Mumbai.
propositions.quote: The Appellants argue that the RPD erred regarding its credibility determinations and that there is no IFA for them in Mumbai.

propositions.text: I agree the RPD erred on credibility but find a viable IFA in Mumbai exists.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Appellants that the RPD erred in its credibility determinations. Nevertheless, I find that they do have a viable IFA in Mumbai.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found credibility and IFA issues; appellants argue errors; the court agrees on credibility error but finds viable IFA in Mumbai.

propositions.text: I dismiss the appeal and find the RPD correct that appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
propositions.quote: I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.

propositions.text: Evidence under s. 110(4) of IRPA is accepted.
propositions.quote: NEW EVIDENCE The evidence under s. 110(4) of IRPA is accepted

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal, agrees RPD's refugee and protection findings, and accepts new evidence under IRPA s.110(4).

propositions.text: The appellants seek to enter a news article titled 'Covid Third Wave Here Already,' Says Mumbai Mayor.
propositions.quote: The Appellants are seeking to enter an article on appeal entitled "'Covid Third Wave Here Already,' Says Mumbai Mayor."

paragraphs.summary: The appellants seek to enter a news article about Mumbai's Covid third wave.

propositions.text: Evidence can be accepted if it arose after RPD decision, was not reasonably available, or could not reasonably have been brought before RPD.
propositions.quote: According to the law, I can only accept evidence that: (i) arose after the RPD decision; or (ii) was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or (iii) that you could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision.

propositions.text: If evidence meets these requirements, it must be new, credible, and relevant to be accepted.
propositions.quote: If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible, and relevant before I can accept it.

paragraphs.summary: The court states legal criteria for accepting new evidence on appeal: timing, availability, and newness, credibility, relevance.

propositions.text: The article arose after RPD decision and is new, relevant, and credible from a reputable news source.
propositions.quote: The Appellants are attempting to enter an article into evidence that arose after the RPD rendered its decision, given that the RPD decision was rendered on June 29, 2021, while the article is dated September 7, 2021. I find that this article is new and relevant, given that it contains information about the current country conditions in Mumbai. I also find that this article is credible, given that it appears to be an article from a reputable news source.

propositions.text: I accept this article into the appeal record.
propositions.quote: As such, I accept this evidence into the appeal record.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the article new, relevant, credible, and accepts it into the appeal record.

propositions.text: An oral hearing is considered under s.110(6) IRPA when new evidence is admitted on appeal.
propositions.quote: Given that I have admitted new evidence on appeal, I must consider whether an oral hearing is necessary under s. 110(6) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

propositions.text: An oral hearing is not required as new evidence does not raise serious credibility issues central to the decision.
propositions.quote: Having reviewed the new evidence and the record, I find that an oral hearing is not required in this appeal because the new evidence does not raise a serious issue about the Appellants' credibility that is central to the decision that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting their claims.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no oral hearing necessary as new evidence does not raise serious credibility issues central to the decision.

propositions.text: My role is to review all evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.
propositions.quote: My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.

propositions.text: The RPD found credibility and IFA were determinative issues.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that credibility and IFA were both determinative issues.

propositions.text: I will consider credibility and IFA issues in turn.
propositions.quote: I will consider each of these in turn.

paragraphs.summary: The court states its role to review evidence and notes RPD found credibility and IFA determinative, which it will consider.

propositions.text: The RPD had credibility concerns about PA's vague and speculative testimony about Q branch.
propositions.quote: The RPD raised several issues around which it had credibility concerns, including that the PA gave vague and speculative testimony about the Q branch which it found "raises a credibility concern."

propositions.text: The RPD found PA's vague testimony about monitoring after arrest further raised credibility concerns.
propositions.quote: The RPD also found that the PA only gave vague and speculative testimony about whether he was monitored after his arrest which "further raises the Panel's concerns as to the Claimant's credibility."

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found credibility concerns due to PA's vague and speculative testimony about Q branch and monitoring after arrest.

propositions.text: The RPD found inconsistent reasons for PA's failure to report to police and doubted the incident occurred.
propositions.quote: The RPD also found that the PA gave inconsistent reasons for failing to report to police following his release, whether it was because his cousin warned him that his uncle had not returned from such a visit, or whether it was because he knew several people that didn't come back from similar visit. The RPD found that his testimony was neither plausible nor credible and raised a doubt as to whether this incident ever occurred.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found PA gave inconsistent reasons for not reporting to police and doubted the incident occurred.

propositions.text: The RPD was concerned about lack of corroboration for police interest during PA's UK stay.
propositions.quote: The RPD was also concerned about the lack of corroboration regarding the police interest in him after he travelled to the UK.

propositions.text: PA testified family was asked about his whereabouts but no proof or corroboration was provided.
propositions.quote: When asked about police interest in him during this time, the PA testified that they asked his family about his whereabouts but there was no proof of this, as there are no records of this visit, and his parents could not provide corroboration, as they were old and it was hard for them to write as they were not well educated.

propositions.text: RPD noted PA's wife remained home and doubted why no confirmation from family was provided.
propositions.quote: The RPD noted that the PA's wife remained in their home at the time and was not persuaded that some form of confirmation of the alleged police visit from family members could not have been provided.

propositions.text: RPD found PA's explanation raised doubt about the alleged police visit.
propositions.quote: As such, the RPD found that the PA's explanation "raises a doubt as to the alleged police visit."

paragraphs.summary: The RPD doubted PA's claim of police interest during UK stay due to lack of corroboration and implausible explanation.

propositions.text: RPD found inconsistency about whether authorities spoke to PA before action against XXXX XXXX and drew negative inference.
propositions.quote: The RPD further found that there was an inconsistency as to whether the authorities spoke to him or not before taking action against the XXXX XXXX. The RPD drew a negative inference as to the inconsistency in the PA's testimony on this point.

propositions.text: RPD had cumulative credibility concerns and doubted integrity of PA's testimony about confrontation with XXXX owners.
propositions.quote: The RPD also noted that, because of its "cumulative concerns as to the credibility of the claimant's allegations, the panel has some doubt as to the integrity of the claimant's testimony concerning his confrontation with XXXX owners."

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found inconsistencies and cumulative credibility concerns, doubting PA's testimony integrity about confrontation with XXXX owners.

propositions.text: RPD had serious doubts about PA's allegations of jeopardy in India.
propositions.quote: The RPD noted that it had serious doubts as to the integrity of the PA's allegations concerning his jeopardy in India.

propositions.text: RPD found an internal flight alternative in Mumbai if appellants feared safety in Tamil Nadu.
propositions.quote: However, it found that if the Appellants were concerned about their safety in Tamil Nadu, there was an IFA for them in Mumbai.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD doubted PA's jeopardy allegations but found a viable internal flight alternative in Mumbai.

propositions.text: Appellants argue RPD did not clearly state if it made a negative credibility finding.
propositions.quote: The Appellants argue that the RPD did not clearly state if it reached a negative credibility finding.

propositions.text: Appellants argue RPD erred by not explicitly stating credibility was undermined and failing to make clear negative findings.
propositions.quote: Further, the Appellants argue that the RPD should have explicitly stated if their credibility was undermined and that it erred in failing to make negative findings of credibility in clear and unmistakable terms.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue RPD failed to clearly state negative credibility findings and erred in not making explicit credibility findings.

propositions.text: Appellants argue RPD erred finding PA's explanation for not attending police invitation implausible.
propositions.quote: Regarding the RPD's concern about the PA's explanation for failing to attend the police invitation, the Appellants argue that the RPD erred in finding the PA's chain of reasoning implausible.

propositions.text: PA testified cousin warned him uncle never returned after police visit; RPD erred in ignoring this explanation.
propositions.quote: Rather, the PA testified that his cousin had told him that an uncle of his reported to the police as requested and was never again seen. The RPD erred in failing to consider this explanation for his failure to attend.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue RPD erred in finding PA's explanation implausible and ignoring cousin's warning about uncle's disappearance.

propositions.text: Appellants allege RPD erred finding implausible that police invited PA rather than arresting him.
propositions.quote: The Appellants allege that the RPD made several credibility errors, such as finding it implausible that Indian police would invite the PA to come into the police station rather than just arresting him.

propositions.text: Appellants argue RPD erroneously asked PA to speculate about agents of persecution's actions.
propositions.quote: The Appellants also argue that the RPD erroneously asked the PA to speculate regarding the actions of the agents of persecution (AOP).

paragraphs.summary: Appellants allege RPD erred in finding police invitation implausible and wrongly asked PA to speculate about persecutors' actions.

propositions.text: Appellants argue PA's evidence was internally consistent.
propositions.quote: The Appellants argue that the PA's evidence was generally internally consistent.

propositions.text: NDP corroborates police human rights abuses and corruption in India, supporting plausibility of false arrest.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, they argue that the National Documentation Package (NDP) corroborates that the police in India are responsible for human rights abuses. Moreover, the documentary evidence notes that Indian police are corrupt and, as such, it is plausible that the PA was subject to a false arrest as alleged.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue PA's evidence is consistent and corroborated by NDP showing police abuses and corruption, making false arrest plausible.

propositions.text: RPD found inconsistency about whether PA was interviewed before action against company; PA testified differently to RPD and counsel
propositions.quote: The Appellants note that the RPD found that there was an inconsistency as to whether the PA had been interviewed by authorities in relation to the complaint that was made against XXXX XXXX prior to them taking action against the company. While the PA testified to the RPD that he was not interviewed before the action occurred, he testified to counsel that he was interviewed prior.

propositions.text: RPD did not make a negative credibility finding based on this inconsistency
propositions.quote: However, the PA notes that the RPD did not make a negative credibility finding on this basis.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellants note the RPD found an inconsistency about PA's interview but did not make a negative credibility finding on it.

propositions.text: RPD raised credibility concerns but failed to make clear, consequential credibility findings
propositions.quote: While the RPD presents several areas of testimony that raised credibility concerns, it nevertheless failed to make any concrete decisions about the consequences or outcomes of these concerns.

propositions.text: RPD must make credibility findings that are clear and consequential
propositions.quote: it is nevertheless incumbent on the RPD to make credibility findings that are clear and consequential.

propositions.text: RPD's credibility findings include vague testimony raising concerns, doubts about incidents, negative inference on inconsistency, and serious doubts about claimant's allegations
propositions.quote: The RPD's credibility findings include that: a. his vague and speculative testimony "raises a credibility concern" (para. 15); b. his vague and speculative testimony about being monitored "raises ... concern as to [his] credibility" (para. 16); c. his testimony was neither plausible nor credible and "raises as [sic] doubt as to whether this incident ever occurred" (para. 17); d. his explanation for a lack of corroborative evidence "raises a doubt as to the alleged police visit" (para. 20); e. the inconsistency about whether the police spoke to him before taking action against XXXX leads the panel to draw a "negative inference as to the inconsistency in the claimant's testimony" (para. 22); f. "In the context of the panel's cumulative concerns as to the credibility of the claimant's allegations, the panel has some doubt as to the integrity of the claimant's testimony concerning his confrontation with XXXX owners." (para. 23); g. The RPD has "serious doubts as to the integrity of the Claimant's allegations concerning his jeopardy in India." (para. 26).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RPD raised credibility concerns but failed to make clear, consequential findings as required, listing RPD's various credibility doubts.

propositions.text: RPD had several concerns about PA's credibility but failed to explain consequences of concerns
propositions.quote: Based on a reading of the decision, it is abundantly clear that the RPD has several concerns about the PA's credibility. However, despite its obvious concerns, the RPD failed to explain the direct consequences of such concerns

propositions.text: RPD only made one real credibility finding: negative inference on inconsistency, but failed to explain its scope or consequence
propositions.quote: Rather, the only real credibility finding made by the RPD was when it drew a negative inference regarding an inconsistency in the claimant's testimony. However, the RPD then failed to explain the consequence of this negative inference

propositions.text: RPD failed to make negative credibility findings clearly and comprehensibly as required
propositions.quote: despite noting that credibility was one of the determinative issues in this case, the RPD failed to make its negative credibility findings clearly and comprehensibly as required.

propositions.text: It is difficult to review RPD's credibility concerns because they did not lead to consequential findings
propositions.quote: It is difficult to review the RPD's credibility concerns in this instance, given that its obvious concerns did not lead to consequential findings.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RPD had credibility concerns but failed to explain their consequences or make clear findings, making review difficult.

propositions.text: Court agrees with RPD that there was inconsistency about police approach before action against XXXX
propositions.quote: I agree with the RPD that there was an inconsistency related to whether the PA was approached by the police before it took action against XXXX.

propositions.text: Court finds inconsistency in PA's evidence about why he did not attend police station when summoned
propositions.quote: I also find that there was an inconsistency in the PA's evidence about why he did not attend the police station when summoned

propositions.text: Court does not find these inconsistencies sufficient to find PA not credible or events did not occur
propositions.quote: However, I do not find that these inconsistencies are sufficient to reach a finding that the PA isn't credible or to find that these events did not occur as alleged.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with RPD on some inconsistencies but finds them insufficient to discredit PA or deny events occurred.

propositions.text: Several RPD credibility concerns stemmed from speculative testimony
propositions.quote: several of the RPD's credibility concerns were a consequence of the speculative nature of the PA's testimony.

propositions.text: RPD asked PA questions requiring speculation about events he was not present for
propositions.quote: the RPD asked the PA questions that required him to speculate. For instance, the RPD asked the PA who told the police about his 2007 arrest

propositions.text: It is unfair to discredit PA's testimony for speculation when RPD asked speculative questions
propositions.quote: Consequently, it is unfair to discredit the PA's testimony on this basis.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RPD's credibility concerns arose from speculative testimony, but RPD's questions required speculation, so discrediting PA on that basis is unfair.

propositions.text: RPD erred in implausibility findings as such findings should be made only in clearest cases
propositions.quote: I also find that the RPD erred in reaching its implausibility findings in this instance, given that the case law is clear that implausibility findings should be made only in the clearest of cases.

propositions.text: RPD's decision is unclear on what it finds implausible
propositions.quote: the RPD's decision is unclear as to what exactly it finds implausible.

propositions.text: Court does not find police inviting PA to attend station instead of arresting him implausible
propositions.quote: I do not find that the police inviting the PA to attend the police station rather than simply arresting him is implausible.

propositions.text: Court does not find PA's testimony about why he didn't attend police station implausible
propositions.quote: Similarly, I do not find that the PA's testimony about why he didn't attend the police station is implausible.

propositions.text: RPD's implausibility finding is not clear and cannot stand
propositions.quote: the alleged implausibility noted by the RPD is certainly not clear on its face. As such, this finding cannot stand.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RPD erred in unclear implausibility findings, which are not supported and cannot stand.

propositions.text: Court does not find RPD's credibility findings correct because RPD failed to specify conclusions from concerns
propositions.quote: I do not find that the RPD's credibility findings are correct in this case for the reasons noted above, and especially because it failed to specify what conclusions it drew from these concerns.

propositions.text: Identifying concerns is important but explaining consequences on credibility is equally important, which RPD failed to do
propositions.quote: Indeed, identifying these concerns is important, but it is just as important to explain the consequences of these concerns on the credibility of a given event, allegation, or the Appellant's overall credibility which the RPD failed to do.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes RPD's credibility findings are incorrect because it failed to specify conclusions or consequences of concerns.

propositions.text: Court finds insufficient credibility concerns to overcome presumption of truth
propositions.quote: Based on my own review of the record, I do not find that there are sufficient credibility concerns to overcome the presumption of truth.

propositions.text: Credibility is not a determinative issue in this case
propositions.quote: As such, I find that credibility is not a determinative issue in this case.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds insufficient credibility concerns to overcome presumption of truth; credibility is not determinative.

propositions.text: Court agrees with RPD that the determinative issue is an internal flight alternative (IFA) in Mumbai
propositions.quote: However, I agree with the RPD find that the determinative issue in this case is an IFA in Mumbai.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with RPD that the key issue is the internal flight alternative in Mumbai.

propositions.text: Test for viable IFA has two prongs: no serious possibility of persecution or risk, and unreasonableness of seeking refuge there
propositions.quote: The test to determine whether a viable IFA exists has two prongs: (i) There is no serious possibility of the Appellants being persecuted or subjected, on a balance of probabilities, to a danger of torture or to a risk to their lives or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in the proposed IFA; and (ii) Conditions in the IFA area are such that it would not be unreasonable, in all the circumstances, including those particular to them, for the Appellants to seek refuge there.

paragraphs.summary: The test for a viable IFA requires no serious risk of persecution and that it is reasonable to seek refuge there.

propositions.text: Once IFA proposed, burden is on appellants to show it is unsafe or unreasonable
propositions.quote: Once the issue of an IFA has been proposed to the Appellants, the burden is on them to demonstrate that the proposed IFA is either unsafe or unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The burden is on appellants to prove the proposed IFA is unsafe or unreasonable.

propositions.text: RPD found appellants' family not contacted by AOP since departure and appellants lack profile to attract police interest
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the Appellants' family had not been contacted by the AOP since their departure and that the Appellants did not have a sufficient profile to attract the interest of regional Indian police forces.

propositions.text: RPD noted Mumbai population approx. 13 million and distance from Tamil Nadu over 1000 km
propositions.quote: It also noted that the population of Mumbai is approximately 13 million and that Mumbai is more than 1 000 kilometres from Tamil Nadu.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found no police interest in appellants and noted Mumbai's large population and distance from Tamil Nadu.

propositions.text: RPD found no evidence of criminal case, warrant, or FIR against PA
propositions.quote: Moreover, the RPD noted that no evidence was tendered indicating that a criminal case had been registered in the PA's name, or that a warrant or First Information Report (FIR) had been issued.

propositions.text: RPD found PA had no evidence of police pursuit in three years away from India
propositions.quote: In addition, the RPD noted that the PA had no evidence of any pursuit by the police in the three years he has been away from India.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found no evidence of criminal case or police pursuit against PA in three years.

propositions.text: RPD found police under state jurisdiction with little interstate communication except major crimes
propositions.quote: The RPD further noted that the police are under state jurisdiction, and the objective evidence indicates that there is little interstate police communication except for cases of major crime.

propositions.text: RPD found appellants would not be located via CCTNS or Aadhaar numbers
propositions.quote: It also found that the Appellants would not be located because of the CCTNS or their Aadhaar numbers.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found limited interstate police communication and that appellants would not be located via CCTNS or Aadhaar.

propositions.text: RPD found no evidence Tamil Nadu authorities interested in pursuing appellants or Mumbai authorities contacting Tamil Nadu
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the RPD found that there was no evidence before it that the authorities in Tamil Nadu have any interest in pursuing the Appellants or that the authorities in Mumbai have any basis to contact Tamil Nadu authorities because of any criminal information obtained.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found no evidence of Tamil Nadu or Mumbai authorities pursuing appellants or sharing criminal info.

propositions.text: Appellants argue RPD failed to consider PA's testimony police searched after relocation to Bangalore
propositions.quote: The Appellants argue that the RPD failed to consider the PA's testimony that police continued to search for them after they relocated to Bangalore.

propositions.text: Appellants argue RPD erred expecting police to create FIR, which may not happen
propositions.quote: Furthermore, they argue that the RPD erred in expecting that the police would create a FIR since they may not for many reasons.

propositions.text: Appellants argue RPD erred finding no risk due to lack of warrants or FIR despite accepting PA's allegations
propositions.quote: Since the RPD accepted the PA's allegations, the Appellants submit that it was an error to find there was no risk because of a lack of corroborating documents.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue RPD failed to consider police search after relocation and erred expecting FIR, thus wrongly finding no risk.

propositions.text: Appellants argue they could be located by AOP through tenant verification, which Mumbai police attempt
propositions.quote: The Appellants argue that they could be located through tenant verification and that the police in Mumbai can do tenant verifications, and even if they don't always have the means to do it, they try.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue they could be located by police through tenant verification in Mumbai.

propositions.text: Appellants argue political pressure causes police communication; new evidence shows 95% police stations linked to CCTNS
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the Appellants argue that political pressure is one of the reasons the police may communicate. Moreover, new evidence indicates that 95% of police stations are now linked to the CCTNS,

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue political pressure causes police communication and most police stations linked to CCTNS.

propositions.text: Appellants argue RPD erred finding viable IFA since PA's problems are with national Q branch and police in Mumbai are corrupt and pose risk
propositions.quote: The Appellants also argue that the RPD erred in finding that there is a viable IFA for them, given that the PA's problems are with the Q branch, which is a national organization. Furthermore, the Appellants argue that an IFA is not appropriate if you fear the police, which they do. The Appellants also argue that the police in Mumbai are also subject to political influence and corruption, and the risk they face from the police includes a risk of torture, mistreatment, and persecution.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue RPD erred finding viable IFA because PA fears national Q branch and corrupt Mumbai police posing risk.

propositions.text: Appellants argue RPD erred by not properly considering new evidence on Aadhaar tracking and security breaches
propositions.quote: The Appellants also argue that the RPD erred by failing to properly consider the new evidence in the June 2021 NDP in finding that it was technically impossible for the government to track citizens using the Aadhaar card.

propositions.text: Appellants argue Aadhaar enrolment is mandatory and can be used as surveillance tool
propositions.quote: The country documentation suggests that Aadhaar enrolment is mandatory, and one source states that a person's Aadhaar number can be "used as a tool of surveillance."

propositions.text: Appellants argue RPD relied on biased source and other sources say tracking by name and movements possible
propositions.quote: The Appellants also argue that the source arguing that people cannot be tracked through Aadhaar is biased, and that another source suggests that you can track someone through their name and movements.

propositions.text: Appellants argue RPD erred finding Aadhaar system never breached and technically secure despite evidence of data sales and police databases
propositions.quote: Moreover, the Appellants argue that the RPD erred in finding that the Aadhaar system had never been breached and is technically secure, given that the documentary evidence suggests that one can buy such information for as little as 10$. Furthermore, country documentation suggests that, since the police are not allowed to access Aadhaar, in some places the police are setting up their own databases. The Appellants argue that this is likely in Mumbai.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue RPD erred by ignoring new evidence on Aadhaar tracking, breaches, biased sources, and police databases.

propositions.text: Appellants argue they will be found due to social media, internet use, and as taxpayers
propositions.quote: The Appellants argue that they will also be found because of their social media and internet use and that they would also be discoverable as taxpayers.

propositions.text: Appellants argue they would be located through contact with family and friends and it's unreasonable to live in hiding
propositions.quote: The Appellants further argue that they would also be located through contact with their family and friends and that it is unreasonable to ask them to forego this contact and live in hiding.

propositions.text: Appellants argue they could be located via electronic means developed for Covid tracking
propositions.quote: The Appellants further argue that they could be located via other electronic means that have been developed for tracking cases of Covid.

propositions.text: Findings on motivation to find the Appellants are unproven
propositions.quote: My findings Motivation to find the Appellants unproven

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue they could be found via social media, contacts, taxes, and Covid tracking; court finds motivation to find them unproven.

propositions.text: Agrees with RPD that insufficient evidence of ongoing police interest in PA for serious persecution possibility in IFA
propositions.quote: I agree with the RPD that there is insufficient evidence of ongoing police interest in the PA such that there is a serious possibility of persecution for him in the IFA.

propositions.text: RPD noted no evidence of criminal case, warrant, or FIR against PA in 2018
propositions.quote: Indeed, as noted by the RPD, there is no evidence before me to show that a criminal case has been registered in the PA's name in 2018, or that a warrant or FIR has been issued.

propositions.text: Police unlikely to conduct countrywide search without legal actions against PA
propositions.quote: I find that the police would be unlikely to conduct a countrywide search to locate the PA in the IFA when no such legal actions have been taken against him by the police.

propositions.text: PA provided no evidence of pursuit or ongoing interest in three years away from India
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the PA has not provided any evidence of any pursuit or ongoing interest in him in the three years he has been away from India.

paragraphs.summary: Court agrees with RPD that no evidence shows ongoing police interest or legal actions against PA, making persecution unlikely in IFA.

propositions.text: Acknowledges PA's testimony of one police attempt to locate him in early 2018
propositions.quote: I acknowledge the PA's testimony that the police sought him once at home after he and his family went into hiding and asked his neighbours and friends about his whereabouts.

propositions.text: One attempt insufficient to find serious police interest or countrywide search likelihood
propositions.quote: I do not find that one attempt to locate the PA in early 2018 is sufficient to ground a finding that the police are interested in the PA such that there is a serious possibility that they would launch a countrywide search to locate him in the IFA.

propositions.text: PA and family relocated to Bangalore for 5.5 months without police countrywide search
propositions.quote: This is especially so since the PA and his family were able to relocate to Bangalore for five and a half months before leaving India, and there is no evidence that the police began a country-wide search for them at the time.

paragraphs.summary: Court acknowledges one police attempt to find PA but finds it insufficient to show serious ongoing interest or countrywide search.

propositions.text: Insufficient evidence authorities in Tamil Nadu have ongoing interest pursuing PA countrywide for persecution in Mumbai
propositions.quote: Having considered the totality of the evidence before me, I find that there is insufficient evidence to demonstrate that the authorities in Tamil Nadu have an ongoing interest in pursuing the PA throughout the country such that he would face a serious possibility of persecution in Mumbai.

propositions.text: No sufficient evidence Q branch police involved in PA's case in 2018 as alleged
propositions.quote: Moreover, I do not find that there is sufficient evidence before me to demonstrate that the Q branch of the police became involved in the PA's case in 2018 as alleged.

propositions.text: PA threatened with potential Q branch involvement but no evidence they became involved during 2018 arrest
propositions.quote: While the PA was threatened with potential Q branch involvement in his case, there is no evidence before me that they became involved in the Appellant's case during his arrest in 2018 as alleged.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds insufficient evidence of ongoing Tamil Nadu police interest or Q branch involvement in PA's case in 2018.

propositions.text: Even if police launched search, unclear if serious possibility Appellants could be located in IFA
propositions.quote: Furthermore, even if I found that the police were to launch a search for the Appellants throughout the country, it is not clear that there is a serious possibility that they could be located in the IFA for the reasons that follow.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds unclear if Appellants could be located in IFA even if police searched nationwide.

propositions.text: Police have mixed success tracking individuals due to non-integrated systems creating 'islands of technology'
propositions.quote: The objective country documentation suggests that police have a mixed record of success in tracking individuals throughout India. Part of the difficulty in tracking individuals throughout the country is because the police systems between districts and states are not integrated, which creates "[i]slands of technology" which can only communicate within a state or district.

propositions.text: Regional police operate independently and communicate mainly for major crimes like terrorism
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the objective country evidence suggests that regional police forces operate independently and generally only communicate to seek out individuals who have been charged with a major crime like terrorism, smuggling, and high-profile organized crime.

propositions.text: Insufficient evidence PA charged with major crime; police interest likely due to failure to report, a minor crime
propositions.quote: As previously noted, although the PA alleges that he is a person of interest for such a crime, there is insufficient evidence before me that the PA has been charged with any such crime. Rather, the police's current interest in him would likely be because of a failure to report to the station as required, which is not a major crime such that it would result in interstate police communication.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds police tracking limited by non-integrated systems and regional independence; PA likely not charged with major crime.

propositions.text: Appellants argue Q branch is national, so no IFA
propositions.quote: The Appellants argue that the Q branch is a national organization, so there is no IFA.

propositions.text: PA dealt with Tamil Nadu police in 2018 and was threatened with Q branch involvement by retired inspector
propositions.quote: However, I note that the PA's evidence is that he dealt with the Tamil Nadu police in 2018, and that he was threatened that his case would be handed over to the Q branch by the retired police inspector who co-owned XXXX XXXX.

propositions.text: Unclear if Q branch handover occurred; PA went into hiding soon after
propositions.quote: However, it is unclear whether this handover ever occurred. Furthermore, the PA went into hiding soon after.

propositions.text: Insufficient evidence Q branch involved in PA's case in 2018 as alleged
propositions.quote: As such, I find that there is insufficient evidence before me to find that the Q branch became involved in the PA's case in 2018 as alleged.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue Q branch is national; court finds insufficient evidence Q branch involved in PA's case in 2018.

propositions.text: PA's evidence shows Q branch is part of Tamil Nadu police and localized
propositions.quote: However, even if they did become involved, the PA's evidence speaks to the localized nature of the Q branch, in stating that the "Q Branch is part of the Tamil Nadu police."

propositions.text: PA's evidence refers to Tamil Nadu Q branch actions, not national scope
propositions.quote: Similarly, the PA's evidence relating to the Q branch speaks of actions taken by "Tamil Nadu 'Q' branch sleuths."

propositions.text: Rejects Appellants' argument that Tamil Nadu Q branch interest means no IFA throughout India
propositions.quote: I do not accept the Appellants' arguments that interest in them by the Tamil Nadu Q branch means that there is no IFA for them throughout India.

propositions.text: Insufficient evidence police involvement extends beyond Tamil Nadu Q branch
propositions.quote: Rather, I find that there is insufficient evidence before me that the police involvement in this case extends to-let alone past-the Q branch in Tamil Nadu.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Q branch is localized to Tamil Nadu and insufficient evidence it extends beyond, rejecting Appellants' no IFA argument.

propositions.text: Cannot find all India unsafe due to PA's Tamil Nadu police interactions without more evidence on Q branch capacity
propositions.quote: Furthermore, one cannot state that the whole of India is automatically unsafe for the Appellants because of the PA's interactions with the police in Tamil Nadu, even if they did come to involve the Q branch as threatened.

propositions.text: More evidence needed on Q branch's interstate police communication capacity
propositions.quote: To make such a finding would require more evidence about the Q branch and its capacity to interact with the various police districts and whether this differs from the regular interstate police communication.

propositions.text: Relies on NDP documentation showing mixed police interstate communication and tracking success depending on crime and political pressure
propositions.quote: Barring such evidence, however, I am left to rely solely on the NDP documentation on police communication. The evidence on interstate communication is mixed and suggests that the police may be able to track and locate persons of interest depending on certain circumstances, including pressure received from political authorities.

propositions.text: Country documentation states police can track persons of interest in heinous crimes with political pressure
propositions.quote: I note that the country documentation specifically states that "police authorities in India are able to track and locate persons of interest, depending on the heinousness of the crime and the pressure received from political authorities. For example, it is possible [for them] to locate a person of interest in cases of rape, murder or armed robbery."

propositions.text: Insufficient evidence PA is person of interest in heinous crimes
propositions.quote: However, there is insufficient evidence before me to find that the PA is a person of interest in any such crimes.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence suggests police systems between districts and states are not integrated and Q branch cannot transcend these issues
propositions.quote: Rather, I find that the documentary evidence suggests that the police systems between districts and states are not integrated, and that there is no evidence before me suggesting that the Q branch in Tamil Nadu is able to transcend these issues.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds whole India not unsafe due to PA's Tamil Nadu police interactions; police tracking depends on crime and political pressure.

propositions.text: Appellants argue they could be located through CCTNS police database linking 95% of police stations
propositions.quote: The Appellants argue that they could be located through the Crime and Criminal Tracking Network and Systems (CCTNS), given that new evidence indicates that 95% of police stations are now linked,

propositions.text: Appellants cite source noting 14,000 police stations linked to CCTNS
propositions.quote: with another source noting that 14 000 police stations are now linked to the database.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue they could be located via CCTNS police database linking most police stations.

propositions.text: Country documentation suggests CCTNS interconnects police stations across India
propositions.quote: The country documentation suggests that the CCTNS police database contains information on crime and criminals that interconnects police stations across the country.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence on CCTNS efficacy is mixed with many limitations
propositions.quote: However, I note that the documentary evidence on the efficacy of the CCTNS is mixed, and the NDP evidence speaks to many limitations of this system.

propositions.text: Police stations still work in silos for criminal information despite CCTNS connection
propositions.quote: Rather, the evidence suggests that police stations in India still work in silos as far as criminal information is concerned.

propositions.text: Police officers continue old paper methods for complaints and FIRs despite CCTNS
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the evidence suggests that, despite being connected to CCTNS, "police officers ... still continue with their old ways for registering complaints and FIRs on paper."

propositions.text: FIR recording in CCTNS varies by state
propositions.quote: Indeed, while FIRs are supposed to be recorded in the CCTNS, whether and how they are recorded varies from state to state.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds CCTNS links police stations but has mixed efficacy; police still use paper methods and work in silos.

propositions.text: CCTNS not yet fully functional countrywide; police unable to trace persons based on it
propositions.quote: Moreover, despite the numbers cited by the Appellants, the evidence continues to cite a source which states that the CCTNS is yet to become functional across the country.

propositions.text: Tracking persons of interest is difficult; police have mixed success
propositions.quote: Another source states that "it has yet to become operational in the sense that the police are still not able to trace a person based on information collected under this project." Similarly, the documentary evidence notes that "tracking persons of interest is difficult and police have a mixed record of success."

propositions.text: No serious possibility Appellants could be located via CCTNS in IFA
propositions.quote: As such, I do not find that there is a serious possibility that the Appellants could be located in the IFA on this basis.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds CCTNS not fully functional and police have mixed success tracking; no serious possibility Appellants located via CCTNS.

propositions.text: Appellants argue tenant verification police checks are mandatory and could locate them
propositions.quote: The Appellants argue that tenant verification police checks are mandatory and could result in their being located in the IFA.

propositions.text: Appellants argue police try tenant verifications despite resource limits
propositions.quote: They argue that the documentary evidence suggests that, even if the police don't always have the resources or ability to conduct tenant verifications, they nevertheless try.

propositions.text: Court finds Appellants misrepresent cited passage and country documentation on tenant verification
propositions.quote: However, I do not find that this is an accurate representation of the specific passage cited by the Appellants, or of the country documentation more generally.

propositions.text: Police in Mumbai and other cities have tried to develop tenant verification databases but are inadequate and not regularly updated
propositions.quote: Indeed, the passage cited by the Appellants notes that the police in Mumbai and other metropolises "have intermittently tried to develop a database and verify the information." However, this passage continues that "to the best of [his] knowledge, this is very inadequate and not updated regularly."

propositions.text: Preponderance of evidence suggests tenant background checks unlikely to occur routinely
propositions.quote: Indeed, I find that the preponderance of the evidence suggests that such background checks are unlikely to occur.

propositions.text: Police Commissioner in Mumbai states police cannot verify all new tenants due to lack of resources
propositions.quote: Rather, the majority of the documentary evidence in the NDP about the occurrence of this process suggests that it does not happen routinely, with a Police Commissioner in Mumbai stating that: "it is impossible for the police to actually verify the identity of all those who rent property ... the police force is not equipped to personally go and check all new tenants."

propositions.text: Other sources note police are ill-equipped and short-staffed to conduct tenant verifications with many forms daily
propositions.quote: Another source notes that the police are too ill-equipped and short-staffed to conduct such verifications when they get over 50 forms per day.

propositions.text: Tenant verification is extremely limited and has several loopholes
propositions.quote: Yet another notes that tenant verification is "extremely limited," with another source stating that the tenant verification system "has several loopholes."

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue tenant verification could locate them; court finds tenant verification is limited, inadequate, and unlikely to occur routinely.

propositions.text: Tenant registration system mandatory in theory but limited in practice
propositions.quote: As such, the country documentation suggests that, although the tenant registration system is mandatory in theory, it is quite limited in practice.

propositions.text: Former Delhi deputy commissioner states tenant verification done for psychological satisfaction, no real follow-up
propositions.quote: Moreover, I note that the documentary evidence also cites a former deputy commissioner of police in Delhi as stating that tenant verification is "done only for the psychological satisfaction, not for actual background check [...] the cops don't make any effort to follow up with the concerned police station of other states."

paragraphs.summary: Court finds tenant registration mandatory but limited; verification done for psychological satisfaction without real follow-up.

propositions.text: No serious possibility police in IFA would contact Tamil Nadu police to locate Appellants via verification process
propositions.quote: For the reasons above, I find that the objective country documentation, when considered in its entirely, suggests that there is not a serious possibility that the police in the IFA would contact the police in Tamil Nadu through the police verification process such that the AOP would become aware of the Appellants' location in the IFA on this basis.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes no serious possibility police in IFA would contact Tamil Nadu police to locate Appellants via verification.

propositions.text: Appellants allege RPD erred on findings about locating them via Aadhaar cards
propositions.quote: The Appellants allege that the RPD erred in its findings related to how they might be located through use of their Aadhaar cards.

propositions.text: Appellants argue Aadhaar enrolment is mandatory and can be used as surveillance tool
propositions.quote: They argue that the country documentation suggests that Aadhaar enrolment is mandatory, and one source states that Aadhaar number can be "used as a tool of surveillance."

propositions.text: Appellants argue source stating tracking via Aadhaar impossible is biased
propositions.quote: The Appellants also argue that the source stating that it is impossible to track people through Aadhaar is biased.

propositions.text: Appellants argue Aadhaar system vulnerable to corruption; info can be bought cheaply
propositions.quote: The Appellants also argue that the RPD failed to accept that the Aadhaar system is vulnerable to corruption, given that some evidence suggests that such information can be purchased for as little as $10.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants allege RPD erred on Aadhaar findings; argue enrolment mandatory, used for surveillance, biased source, and vulnerable to corruption.

propositions.text: Country documentation on tracking via Aadhaar is mixed; some say impossible, others say surveillance tool
propositions.quote: I acknowledge that the country documentation on tracking people through Aadhaar cards is somewhat mixed, given that, while one source states it's impossible, another source states that it can be used as a tool of surveillance.

propositions.text: Police not able to access Aadhaar info for investigations
propositions.quote: Nevertheless, as noted by the Appellants, the country documentation states that the police are not able to access this information for their investigations.

propositions.text: No serious possibility police would break law to access Aadhaar info to locate Appellants
propositions.quote: As such, I do not find that there is a serious possibility that they would be located on this basis, as I do not find that there is sufficient evidence to demonstrate a that the police would break the law to access this information they are not legally entitled to use.

propositions.text: Appellants suggest Mumbai police may have own databases
propositions.quote: The Appellants have also suggested that the police in Mumbai may have started their own databases.

propositions.text: No evidence Mumbai police have started own database; concern speculative
propositions.quote: However, I do not find that there's a serious possibility that the Appellants would be located on this basis either. Rather, I find this concern to be speculative, given that there is no evidence before me that the police in Mumbai have begun to set up their own database as alleged.

propositions.text: Appellants submit Aadhaar system vulnerable to data breaches
propositions.quote: Furthermore, while I note that the Appellants submit that the Aadhaar system is vulnerable to data breaches,

propositions.text: Appellants have not shown data breach or compromise; locating via breach speculative
propositions.quote: I do not find that the Appellants have shown that they could be located through their information being obtained in a data breach. They have not provided evidence to demonstrate that their data has been compromised or breached in any way. As such, their suggestion that they could be located in the IFA because of a data breach is simply speculative.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds mixed Aadhaar tracking evidence; police cannot access info legally; no evidence of Mumbai police database or data breach locating Appellants.

propositions.text: Appellants argue they will be found due to social media and internet use
propositions.quote: I also do not accept the Appellants' argument that they will also be found because of their social media and internet use.

propositions.text: Federal Court in Olusola held limitations on social media use not unreasonable in IFA
propositions.quote: As noted by the Federal Court in Olusola, limitations on the use of social media are not unreasonable in a proposed IFA.

propositions.text: Court held careful social media use expected; burden on Appellants to show risk of AOP locating them
propositions.quote: Indeed, the Court held that it is not wrong to expect a person's use of social media to be careful, and the burden is on the Appellants to provide evidence as to how their careful use of social media would present a risk of the AOP locating them.

propositions.text: Appellants have not demonstrated how careful social media use risks AOP locating them
propositions.quote: I do not find that the Appellants have demonstrated how their careful use of social media would result in a risk of the AOP finding them in this instance.

propositions.text: Appellants' arguments about internet usage risk are speculative
propositions.quote: Similarly, I find the Appellants' arguments that they would be located because of their internet usage more generally to be speculative.

paragraphs.summary: Court rejects Appellants' argument on social media and internet use risk; cites Federal Court precedent and finds arguments speculative.

propositions.text: Appellants argue they would be discoverable as taxpayers
propositions.quote: The Appellants also argue that they would be discoverable as taxpayers.

propositions.text: Appellants failed to provide sufficient evidence how AOP could locate them via tax payment
propositions.quote: However, I find that the Appellants have failed to provide sufficient evidence as to how the AOP in this instance would have the means and ability to locate them in the IFA through their payment of taxes.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue discoverable as taxpayers; court finds insufficient evidence to support this.

propositions.text: Appellants argue AOP will know they are back in India if in contact with family and friends, forcing hiding
propositions.quote: The Appellants argue that the AOP will come to know that they are back in India if they are in contact with their family and friends and that they would have to live in hiding as a result.

propositions.text: Court finds argument speculative; insufficient evidence Appellants must forego contact to avoid AOP detection
propositions.quote: I find this argument is speculative. Rather, I do not find that the Appellants have provided sufficient evidence to demonstrate that they would have to forego contact with their family and friends to prevent the AOP from finding out that they have returned to India and/or where they are located.

propositions.text: No evidence AOP has tried to contact Appellants' friends or family since hiding in Bangalore in 2018
propositions.quote: Indeed, there is no evidence before me of the AOP making efforts to contact the Appellants' friends or family to seek information about them since after they went into hiding in Bangalore in early 2018.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Appellants' argument about contact with family forcing hiding speculative; no evidence AOP contacted family since 2018.

propositions.text: Appellants argue they could be located due to Covid tracking via electronic portal in Karnataka.
propositions.quote: The Appellants have also argued that they could be located because of Covid tracking. They have provided an article that notes that all travellers coming into the state of Karnataka must register on an electronic portal which allows the state to follow them for several days.

propositions.text: Article states tracking occurs in Karnataka, but Mumbai is in Maharashtra, so Covid tracking unlikely to locate Appellants in IFA.
propositions.quote: I note that the article states that this tracking is occurring in the state of Karnataka, while Mumbai is located in the state of Maharashtra. Consequently, I do not find that there is a serious possibility that the Appellants would be located by the AOP in the IFA because of Covid tracking.

propositions.text: Avoiding travel to Karnataka does not make relocation to IFA unreasonable.
propositions.quote: While the Appellants may wish to mitigate any perceived risk by avoiding travel to Karnataka, I do not find that such a limitation means that relocation to the IFA would be unreasonable.

propositions.text: No sufficient evidence that Appellants must download contact tracing app to be located.
propositions.quote: Similarly, I do not find that there is sufficient evidence to show that the Appellants would be required to download the government's contact tracing application such that there is a serious possibility they could be located on this basis.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue Covid tracking could locate them in Karnataka; court finds tracking limited to Karnataka, Mumbai is in Maharashtra, so relocation to IFA is reasonable.

propositions.text: Appellants have not provided sufficient evidence that AOP could locate them in IFA; no serious possibility of being found.
propositions.quote: I do not find that the Appellants have provided sufficient evidence about the AOP's motivation, means, and ability to find them in the IFA such that there is a serious possibility that they could be located in the IFA as alleged.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes Appellants failed to prove serious possibility of being located by AOP in IFA.

propositions.text: RPD found Mumbai is large multi-ethnic city; PA likely to succeed there due to education, business experience, and living abroad.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that Mumbai is a very large multi-ethnic city and found that the PA would be likely to succeed there given that he has a high school education, business experience, and experience living in another country for a long time.

propositions.text: RPD noted PA provided no evidence of difficulty obtaining employment in Mumbai.
propositions.quote: The RPD also noted that the PA provided no evidence that he would have difficulty seeking and obtaining employment in Mumbai.

propositions.text: RPD found PA would likely find employment and support family in Mumbai on balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: As such, the RPD found that the PA would, on a balance of probabilities, be able to find employment in Mumbai and be able to support himself and his family.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found Mumbai suitable for PA to find employment and support family based on education and experience.

propositions.text: Appellants argue IFA unreasonable due to isolation from family, friends, and limited social media/internet use to hide from AOP.
propositions.quote: The Appellants argue that the IFA is unreasonable because they would have to be cut off from family and friends to stay in hiding, and that they would be unable to use social media and would have to limit their internet use to hide from the AOP.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue IFA unreasonable due to social isolation and limited internet use to avoid AOP.

propositions.text: Appellants argue they cannot work due to Covid risk, poor medical system, shortage of supplies, lack of health care, Aadhaar, and support network in IFA.
propositions.quote: The Appellants also argue that they would be unable to work due to a significant risk of contracting Covid given the high number of cases in Mumbai. They further argue that the medical system in India is unable to cope with the pandemic and that there is a shortage of essential supplies. The Appellants also argue that the IFA would be unreasonable because they would lack access to health care, Aadhaar numbers, and a support network.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue Covid risk, poor healthcare, and lack of support make IFA unreasonable.

propositions.text: Court rejects Appellants' claim they must cut off family, social media, or internet to avoid AOP; IFA not unreasonable on this basis.
propositions.quote: I do not find that the Appellants have proven that they would have to be cut off from family and friends and not use social media or the internet to avoid the AOP as alleged. As such, I do not find that the Appellants have proven that the IFA would be unreasonable on this basis.

propositions.text: While relocation without family/friends nearby may be difficult, it does not make IFA unreasonable.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, while I accept that it could be difficult for the Appellants to relocate to an area where they do not have any family or friends close by, I do not find that the Appellants have shown that the IFA would be unreasonable on this basis.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds no proof Appellants must isolate socially; relocation without family nearby not unreasonable.

propositions.text: Appellants argue PA unable to work due to Covid risk in Mumbai.
propositions.quote: The Appellants also argue that the PA would be unable to work due to a significant risk of contracting Covid.

propositions.text: Court finds insufficient evidence that PA cannot work due to Covid; agrees with RPD that PA likely to find work based on education and experience.
propositions.quote: I do not find that they have provided sufficient evidence or arguments to explain why the PA would be unable to work because of Covid. Rather, I agree with the RPD that based on the PA's education and work experience, he would, on a balance of probabilities, be able to find work in the IFA.

propositions.text: Acknowledges Covid third wave in Mumbai but finds insufficient proof it prevents PA from working or makes working unreasonable.
propositions.quote: While I acknowledge the Appellants' evidence about the third wave of Covid in Mumbai having started in September 2021, I don't find that this is sufficient to prove that the PA would be unable to find work, or that it would be unreasonable for him to work in Mumbai on this basis.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue Covid prevents PA working; court finds insufficient evidence and agrees PA likely to find work.

propositions.text: Appellants argue lack of access to health care and Aadhaar numbers makes IFA unreasonable.
propositions.quote: Similarly, I do not find that the Appellants have shown that relocation to the IFA would be unreasonable because they would lack access to health care or Aadhaar numbers as alleged.

propositions.text: Appellants failed to provide sufficient evidence they would have problems obtaining Aadhaar or basic services including health care in IFA.
propositions.quote: Rather, I find that the Appellants have failed to provide sufficient evidence to demonstrate that they would be likely to have problems obtaining an Aadhaar card and basic services, including health care in the IFA.

propositions.text: Burden is on Appellants to prove IFA unreasonable; their arguments on this point are speculative.
propositions.quote: It is their burden to prove that the IFA would be unreasonable on this basis, and I do not find that they have provided sufficient evidence to discharge this burden. Rather, I find their arguments on this point to be speculative.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Appellants failed to prove lack of Aadhaar or health care access; burden is on them and arguments are speculative.

propositions.text: Appellants argue Indian medical system cannot cope with pandemic, especially in Mumbai.
propositions.quote: The Appellants also argue that the medical system in India is unable to cope with the pandemic. They have provided evidence regarding the difficulties created by Covid on the health care system, especially in Mumbai.

propositions.text: Court acknowledges health care system is strained but finds insufficient evidence that Appellants would have difficulty accessing health care in Mumbai making relocation unreasonable.
propositions.quote: I am mindful of this evidence and acknowledge that the evidence provided notes that the health care system is strained. However, I do not find that they have provided sufficient evidence to demonstrate that they-in their specific circumstances-would have difficulties accessing health care in Mumbai such that relocation there would be unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue medical system strained; court acknowledges but finds insufficient evidence it makes relocation unreasonable.

propositions.text: Unreasonableness of IFA requires conditions jeopardizing life and safety with actual and concrete evidence.
propositions.quote: While I acknowledge that there may be some difficulties for the Appellants in relocating to the IFA, a very high threshold exists for the unreasonableness portion of the IFA test. According to the Federal Court, it "requires nothing less than the existence of conditions which would jeopardize the life and safety of a claimant."35 Furthermore, it requires "actual and concrete evidence of such conditions."36

propositions.text: Appellants have not provided actual and concrete evidence of conditions jeopardizing their life and safety if relocated to Mumbai.
propositions.quote: I do not find that the Appellants have provided actual and concrete evidence of any conditions that would, alone or in combination, jeopardize their lives and safety if they relocate to Mumbai.

propositions.text: Appellants have not proven relocation to IFA would be unreasonable in their circumstances.
propositions.quote: Consequently, I find that the Appellants have not proven that a relocation to the IFA would be unreasonable in their circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: Court states high threshold for unreasonableness requires concrete evidence; Appellants failed to prove relocation unreasonable.

propositions.text: Appeal dismissed; RPD decision confirmed that Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
propositions.quote: I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: Court dismisses appeal and confirms RPD decision denying refugee or protection status to Appellants.
